findings.body:
**Do not count a zombie as surviving work.**

If the controller kills a harness-owned child during a drain refusal, the child can remain a zombie until the harness waits for it. Linux still lets the harness read the child's empty `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`. `process_state()` sets `alive=True`, and the refusal check can accept the child's unchanged start time as proof of survival. ([kernel.org](https://www.kernel.org/pub/linux/docs/man-pages/book/man-pages-6.7.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Read the process state and start time from the same `/proc/<pid>/stat` sample. Reject zombie and dead states before reporting the process as alive.
findings.title: Do not count a zombie as surviving work.

findings.body:
**Stop the paused switch if the observation fails.**

If `during()` raises after the pause marker appears, the phase returns an error without terminating or reaping the switch process. It also skips the caller's marker and trigger cleanup. The guest can still have a masked service and a pending journal at that point.

On callback failure, terminate and reap the child before removing the marker. Run the caller's fixture cleanup on that path too. On success, keep releasing the marker only after the observation finishes.
findings.title: Stop the paused switch if the observation fails.

findings.body:
**Match the journaled completions to the fixture log.**

A switch can pass with one new fixture completion and two journal entries whose invocation IDs never appear in the log. `validate_completed()` checks the journal against the pre-switch log, but this check only tests the final runtime. The harvest switches use the same journal validation and only require aggregate log growth.

For each switch, match both journal entries to new log entries by invocation, sequence, unit, runtime, and success. Allow additional fixture completions without letting them stand in for the journaled pair.
findings.title: Match the journaled completions to the fixture log.

findings.body:
**Check fixture files before undoing the negative control.**

The unsafe-metadata case changes the drop-in mode to `0666`. If the controller changes it to `0600` and then returns the expected refusal, `cleanup()` restores the original mode. The final file comparison then passes and hides the controller write.

Capture the file state immediately after the CLI returns and compare it with `mutated_files`. Run cleanup in `finally` so the negative control is undone even if the observation fails.
findings.title: Check fixture files before undoing the negative control.

findings.body:
**Verify that the same waiting start job survives mask and reload.**

The fence seeds a specific waiting start job but later accepts any row containing `crq-repair.service`, after issuing two more start attempts. A different job ID or a stop job can satisfy that check after the original job disappears.

Before issuing the external start attempts, require a successful `list-jobs` observation with the same job ID, unit, `start` type, and `waiting` state. Use the same identity check in the positive cancellation control at Line 2117.
findings.title: Verify that the same waiting start job survives mask and reload.

findings.body:
**Check restoration against the snapshot captured before recovery.**

Both recovery checks load the expected service metadata and timer state from the journal after recovery has rewritten it. If recovery restores mode `0600` instead of `0644` and also changes the journal's snapshot to `0600`, the exact-restoration check passes.

Capture the expected service metadata and timer state from the pending journal before the CLI call. After recovery, compare the fixture to that saved snapshot and use the new journal to verify the terminal outcome.






Also applies to: 1250-1250, 1406-1406, 1418-1418
findings.title: Check restoration against the snapshot captured before recovery.

findings.body:
**Require SIGKILL exit status for the drain interruption check.**

The check at line 1212 accepts any nonzero exit code. A normal refusal from `recover` can return a nonzero code and leave a pending `drained` record unchanged. Lines 1214-1218 then pass, so the case reports an interrupted recovery even when the `drain` kill hook never terminated the process. The proof documentation requires an exact SIGKILL for this case, which appears as rc `-9`. The runner predicate for `recover-kill` has the same gap.

<details>
<summary>Suggested fix</summary>

```diff
-    require(payload["cli"]["rc"] not in (0, None),
-            "interrupted recovery unexpectedly returned success")
+    require(payload["cli"]["rc"] == -9,
+            "interrupted recovery was not terminated by SIGKILL at the drain hook")
```

</details>

Apply the same exact-status predicate to the `recover-kill` entry in `apps/crq-python/ops/vm-unit-switch.py`.
findings.title: Require SIGKILL exit status for the drain interruption check.

findings.body:
**Require the same guest boot ID for a manager restart.**

A guest reboot can change both the manager PID and invocation ID, so it can satisfy `manager_restarted`. A later reboot can then satisfy the separate reboot check. Require nonempty, equal boot IDs on both sides of the manager restart, in addition to the existing manager identity checks.
findings.title: Require the same guest boot ID for a manager restart.

findings.body:
**Protect the VM immediately after spawning it.**

If appending to `commands.jsonl` fails after `Popen` succeeds, `boot()` exits before its cleanup block and before it writes `process.json`. On a fresh run, the outer cleanup has no identity to stop, so QEMU can remain live after the command fails. Move the append into the protected region and make that region stop the process it spawned even if identity persistence fails.
findings.title: Protect the VM immediately after spawning it.

findings.body:
**Reject non-object run metadata before reading `port`.**

If `run.json` contains `[]`, decoding succeeds but `meta.get("port")` raises `AttributeError`. The CLI does not catch it, so `--json boot` produces a traceback on stderr and no JSON artifact. Check that the decoded value is an object and raise a runtime error through the existing JSON handler.

As per coding guidelines, “In machine mode (`--json`) stderr stays empty.”
findings.title: Reject non-object run metadata before reading `port`.

findings.body:
**Allocate the forwarded port at boot, not at preparation.**

If you prepare two runs before booting either, both can store port `2222`: `free_port()` closes its socket before returning. Once the first VM binds that port, the second cannot boot, and retrying reuses the same port. Select the port during launch and retry a bind conflict without changing the first VM’s port.
findings.title: Allocate the forwarded port at boot, not at preparation.

findings.body:
**Do not stop an existing VM when a second boot fails.**

If a run is already live and available memory drops below the boot minimum, a second `boot` fails before it spawns anything. Its cleanup still reads the first invocation’s `process.json` and stops that VM. Refuse to boot a live run, and restrict failure cleanup to the process started by the current invocation.
findings.title: Do not stop an existing VM when a second boot fails.

findings.body:
**Return JSON for every argument error.**

An unknown phase exits 2 through stock `argparse` with no JSON on stdout. A known `--case` that belongs to a different phase exits 1 instead of 2. Route both failures through the same JSON usage handler as an omitted `--case`. Keep exit 1 for failures during phase execution. ([docs.python.org](https://docs.python.org/3.11/library/argparse.html?utm_source=openai))

As per coding guidelines, “Every operation invocation writes machine-readable JSON to stdout” and exit code 2 is for an “arg error.”
    


Also applies to: 899-901
findings.title: Return JSON for every argument error.

findings.body:
**Bind provenance to the host script the interpreter runs.**

The interpreter can start with source A, then read source B from `__file__` after a checkout changes the working tree during image fetch or preparation. If the pin names B, the comparison passes and the report retains B even though A ran. Launch from the same pinned, immutable snapshot that the report retains. Reading the working tree earlier would narrow the window but would not prove which bytes the interpreter loaded.
findings.title: Bind provenance to the host script the interpreter runs.

findings.body:
**Filter the activation wait by the released runtime.**

`wait_completions` counts every entry in the repair completion log, not only entries for the runtime under test. It also says "released-runtime completion" in its failure message, so the predicate does not match its stated purpose. A completion from the prior runtime can satisfy the wait before the released runtime has completed. The later check then fails the run, even when the released runtime completes within the 60-second bound.

The window exists because the `before` snapshot is taken before the switch masks the service. A timer tick can run the prior service in that window. Count only entries for `spec["runtime"]`, both in the baseline and in the wait:

```diff
-def wait_completions(minimum, label):
+def wait_completions(minimum, label, runtime=None):
     deadline = time.time() + 60
-    while len(read_completions(REPAIR_COMPLETIONS)) < minimum:
+    while len([item for item in read_completions(REPAIR_COMPLETIONS)
+               if runtime is None or item.get("runtime") == runtime]) < minimum:
         require(time.time() < deadline,
                 label + " produced no released-runtime completion in the bound")
         time.sleep(0.2)
```

```diff
     if spec["hook"] != "start-after-service":
-        wait_completions(len(before["repair_completions"]) + 1,
-                         "activation " + case)
+        released_before = [item for item in before["repair_completions"]
+                           if item.get("runtime") == spec["runtime"]]
+        wait_completions(len(released_before) + 1, "activation " + case,
+                         spec["runtime"])
```
findings.title: Filter the activation wait by the released runtime.

findings.body:
**Stage each download in a private temporary file.**

`download()` always stages to the fixed path `<name>.part`, and it opens that path with `"wb"`. Two cold-cache fetches for the same cache therefore write to the same file. The second open truncates the first fetch's staged bytes. If the second open happens after the first fetch hashes the file and before the rename, the first fetch publishes truncated bytes at `image_path` and still returns `sums_verified: true`. The shared `sums.part` path has the same problem. A later warm-path fetch rehashes the cached image and can reject it, so recovery can require manually deleting the cache file.

Give each download its own staging file in the destination directory. Each fetch then writes, hashes and renames only its own bytes. The rename stays atomic because the staging file is on the same filesystem. Locking the cache across selection and publication is optional. A lock prevents duplicate downloads, but it is not required to fix this race.

<details>
<summary>Suggested fix</summary>

```diff
 def download(url: str, destination: pathlib.Path, timeout: float = 120) -> str:
-    """Download to a sibling ``.part`` and fsync before replacing."""
-    part = destination.with_name(destination.name + ".part")
-    with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=timeout) as response, \
-            part.open("wb") as handle:
-        while True:
-            chunk = response.read(1 << 20)
-            if not chunk:
-                break
-            handle.write(chunk)
-        handle.flush()
-        os.fsync(handle.fileno())
-    return str(part)
+    """Download to a private sibling staging file and fsync before replacing."""
+    with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=timeout) as response:
+        descriptor, name = tempfile.mkstemp(
+            dir=destination.parent, prefix=destination.name + ".", suffix=".part")
+        with os.fdopen(descriptor, "wb") as handle:
+            while True:
+                chunk = response.read(1 << 20)
+                if not chunk:
+                    break
+                handle.write(chunk)
+            handle.flush()
+            os.fsync(handle.fileno())
+    return name
```

The fix needs `import tempfile` if the module does not already import it. `fetch_sums` calls the same `download()`, so this one change covers the checksum file too.

</details>
findings.title: Stage each download in a private temporary file.
